title: Pre-contract searches and enquiries
subtitle: What a local search, drainage search, environmental search and chancel check are each actually for
objectives: Explain what the standard local authority search (CON29/CON29O) and the Local Land Charges Register actually reveal, and what they do not
Distinguish what a drainage and water search, an environmental search and a chancel repair search are each checking for
Apply the law of misrepresentation to a seller's inaccurate answer on pre-contract enquiries

leadingAuthorities.role: Governs registration and searching of local land charges (LLC1)
Governs liability where a seller's pre-contract answers turn out to be false

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Most students can list 'local search, drainage search, environmental search' as a set of boxes to tick. The examinable skill is knowing what each search is actually capable of telling you — and, just as importantly, what it cannot — so that a fact pattern describing a specific risk points you to the right search rather than a generic one.

profileHooks.weakApplication: You can name the searches. This lesson tests whether you can match a described risk — flooding, a former petrol station, an old church nearby — to the specific search or enquiry that actually addresses it.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Parts 1 and 2 and be precise about what CON29, CON29O and LLC1 each cover — students regularly conflate the two and lose marks on a straightforward recall point.

overview.hook: A buyer's solicitor who skips the drainage search because 'the property obviously has a working toilet' has misunderstood the point of the exercise entirely. Pre-contract searches aren't there to confirm the obvious — they exist to surface the risks that are invisible on an ordinary viewing: a road-widening scheme, a leaking underground tank from decades ago, an ancient liability to repair a church roof miles from the property itself.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 24 September 2026. Local authority search formats (CON29/CON29O) are periodically revised by the Law Society and Local Government Association; the underlying statutory and common law framework covered here is stable.

parts.heading: The local authority search: CON29 and the Local Land Charges Register
parts.voice: practical — explains the document as a solicitor would order and read it
body: The standard local authority search has two components submitted together. The LLC1 form searches the Local Land Charges Register, maintained under the Local Land Charges Act 1975, and returns registered charges such as planning permissions and conditions, tree preservation orders, listed building status, and financial charges the local authority has registered against the land.

The CON29 form (Enquiries of Local Authority) sits alongside LLC1 and asks a standard set of questions that go beyond what is formally registered as a land charge — road adoption status, whether the property is in a conservation area, planning enforcement history, and proposals for nearby road schemes are all typical CON29 answers. Where a specific risk is flagged, an optional CON29O adds further enquiries, for example about contaminated land notices or common land registration.

It is worth being precise about the boundary here: the LLC1 register is a fixed, conclusive register of what has actually been formally registered, giving a right to compensation if the register is inaccurate; the CON29 answers are the local authority's best information in response to specific questions and do not carry the same statutory guarantee. A solicitor advising a client should not present the two as interchangeable.

components.definition: A charge or restriction registered against land under the Local Land Charges Act 1975 — for example a planning condition, tree preservation order or financial charge — searchable on LLC1 and binding on successive owners regardless of whether they knew of it.

interaction.prompt: A buyer's solicitor wants to check whether a tree preservation order is registered against the property. Which form should they rely on?
options: LLC1
CON29 only, since tree preservation orders are never registered as local land charges
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Tree preservation orders are a classic example of a registered local land charge, searched for on LLC1.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Tree preservation orders are registered local land charges — that puts them squarely within the LLC1 search, not just the CON29 enquiries.

parts.heading: Drainage, water, environmental and chancel — four searches, four different risks
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style comparison students will return to
body: Beyond the local authority search sit several further enquiries, each aimed at a distinct risk that a viewing of the property cannot reveal. Confusing what each one covers is one of the most common errors in practice, and one of the most tested in an exam setting.

A drainage and water search (commonly known by its CON29DW form) confirms whether the property is connected to mains water and mains foul and surface water drainage, and shows the approximate route of public sewers relative to the property — critical where a client plans an extension, since building over or near a public sewer normally requires the water company's consent.

An environmental search assesses contaminated land risk and flood risk by reference to historical land use (for example a former petrol station, tannery or landfill site) and environmental agency data — it is a risk-screening exercise, not a guarantee, and a positive result typically leads to further investigation rather than an automatic refusal to proceed.

A chancel repair search addresses a genuinely obscure but real liability: in some parishes, owners of land that was historically rectorial glebe land can be liable to contribute to the repair of the parish church chancel, even where the land has no obvious physical connection to the church at all. The search checks historical records for this liability, and where a risk is identified, indemnity insurance is the conventional practical solution rather than further investigation.

components.label: Four searches, four questions
points: Drainage and water search — is the property connected to mains services, and where do public sewers run relative to it?
Environmental search — is there a risk of contamination or flooding based on historical land use and agency data?
Chancel repair search — could this land carry an ancient liability to contribute to a parish church's repair?
Local authority search (LLC1/CON29) — what is formally registered, and what does the council say about planning, roads and enforcement?

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario that a drainage and water search — rather than an environmental search — is specifically designed to reveal.
interaction.scenarioText: A client wants to build a rear extension. The site was previously used as a small engineering workshop, and the client is also concerned about whether a public sewer runs beneath the proposed extension footprint.
tappableSpans: previously used as a small engineering workshop
whether a public sewer runs beneath
interaction.correctSpan: whether a public sewer runs beneath
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. The route of public sewers relative to the property is exactly what a drainage and water search shows — the former workshop use is instead a prompt for an environmental search.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The former industrial use points to contamination risk (environmental search). The sewer route question is the drainage and water search's specific job — look again for that fact.

parts.heading: Pre-contract enquiries: the questions searches don't answer
parts.voice: case-narrative — walks through a live scenario before naming the doctrine
body: Searches address matters of public record and infrastructure. They cannot tell a buyer whether the seller has had a dispute with a neighbour about the boundary fence, or whether a leak in the roof was ever repaired. That gap is filled by pre-contract enquiries, typically raised on the Law Society's standard Property Information Form (TA6), supplemented by bespoke enquiries where the property or the buyer's plans raise something unusual.

Imagine a seller completes the TA6 form and answers 'No' to a question asking whether there have been any disputes with neighbours, when in fact a boundary dispute was raised and only recently settled informally. The buyer proceeds to purchase in reliance on that answer, then discovers the dispute after completion when the neighbour raises it again.

This is a live misrepresentation problem, not merely a broken promise. If the seller's false statement of fact induced the buyer to enter the contract, the buyer may have a claim under the Misrepresentation Act 1967 — for rescission of the contract (where still possible) and/or damages, with the measure and availability of remedies depending on whether the misrepresentation was fraudulent, negligent, or wholly innocent. This is precisely why sellers are advised to answer pre-contract enquiries with genuine care, and why 'I didn't think it mattered' is not a defence to an inaccurate answer of fact.

components.definition: A false statement of fact made by the seller (commonly in pre-contract enquiries) that induces the buyer to enter the contract, giving rise to potential remedies of rescission and/or damages under the Misrepresentation Act 1967, depending on the seller's state of mind when the statement was made.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that a seller who genuinely forgot about a settled boundary dispute, and answered 'No' in good faith, can still face a misrepresentation claim?
sliderLabels: Liability is still possible even without dishonesty
interaction.explanation: An innocent misrepresentation still allows a claim, though the available remedies differ from a fraudulent or negligent one — the Misrepresentation Act 1967 does not require dishonesty for liability to arise, only a false statement of fact that induced the contract.

parts.heading: Reading a CON29 answer against the statutory register
parts.voice: direct — sets up the distinction the tests will probe
body: It's worth returning to the LLC1/CON29 distinction with one more layer of precision, because exam questions often hinge on it. The Local Land Charges Act 1975 creates a genuine public register: an entry on it is conclusive as a matter of registration, and a search certificate that fails to reveal a registered charge gives the person who relied on it a statutory right to compensation for loss suffered as a result.

CON29 answers, by contrast, are the local authority's response to a standard set of enquiries drawing on its own records — useful and generally reliable, but not backed by the same statutory compensation regime. If a CON29 answer turns out to be wrong because the council's own records were simply incomplete, the buyer's recourse is far less clear-cut than where an actual registered charge was missed from the LLC1 search.

A solicitor who treats 'the local search came back clean' as a single undifferentiated fact, without being able to say which part of it carries a statutory guarantee, has not actually understood what the client is paying for.

components.text: Where a search of the register maintained by any registering authority... discloses no subsisting registration of a matter of which registration is required or is not affected by section 1(5) above, then... any person who suffers loss in consequence of that failure... shall be entitled to compensation.
elements: An official search is made of the register
The search fails to reveal a subsisting registered charge
The person searching (or on whose behalf the search was made) suffers loss as a result
Compensation is payable for that loss

interaction.prompt: A registered tree preservation order is not revealed by an official LLC1 search due to an administrative error at the registering authority. The buyer fells a protected tree and is prosecuted, suffering financial loss as a result. What follows under s 10 of the Local Land Charges Act 1975?
options: No remedy exists, because CON29 and LLC1 answers are never compensable
The buyer has a statutory right to compensation for the loss caused by the registering authority's failure to reveal the registered charge
The buyer must sue the seller for misrepresentation instead, since the local authority owes no duty at all
The tree preservation order becomes unenforceable once it is missed on a search
interaction.explanation: This is exactly the situation s 10 addresses: a subsisting registered local land charge not revealed by an official search gives rise to a statutory compensation right against the registering authority for resulting loss.

parts.heading: Building the search bundle to fit the transaction
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the practical judgement call before resolving it
body: Here's the question a competent trainee has to answer on every file, not just recite an answer to: which searches does this specific transaction actually need? The standard bundle — local authority search, drainage and water search, and an environmental search — is close to universal. Chancel repair searches have become less routine since many parishes have now extinguished or insured against the risk, but a solicitor who skips the check without any basis for doing so, on a property in a parish where the risk is live, has not met the standard of a reasonably competent conveyancer.

The skill being tested is matching a described risk to the right response — not memorising an unvarying checklist. A flood risk near a river points hard towards an environmental search with a flood-specific element; a proposed large extension over open garden land points towards checking the drainage search's sewer map with real care, not just confirming the box was ticked.

And running underneath every one of these searches sits the same underlying discipline as pre-contract enquiries: none of this is optional box-ticking. Each search or enquiry exists because a specific category of risk cannot otherwise be discovered before exchange, and a solicitor who advises a client to exchange contracts without addressing an obviously relevant risk is exposed to a negligence claim quite separately from anything the seller may or may not have disclosed.

components.title: Matching a risk to the right search or enquiry
components.description: A quick decision aid for choosing which pre-contract search or enquiry addresses a described risk.

nodes.label: What is the specific risk described in the facts?
Planning history, road adoption, listed status, TPOs → LLC1/CON29
Mains connection or sewer route near a planned extension → drainage and water search
Former industrial use or flood-prone location → environmental search
Property in an old parish, ancient rectorial land → chancel repair search
Something only the seller would know (disputes, defects, past works) → pre-contract enquiries (TA6) — misrepresentation risk if answered falsely

components.textAlternative: Match the risk in the facts to the right tool: planning history, road adoption or tree preservation orders point to LLC1/CON29; mains connection or sewer routes near planned works point to a drainage and water search; former industrial use or flood exposure points to an environmental search; an old parish with historically rectorial land points to a chancel repair search; and anything only the seller could know, such as disputes or past defects, is addressed through pre-contract enquiries, with misrepresentation exposure if the seller answers falsely.

interaction.prompt: A property sits on a site that was a working dry cleaner's until the 1990s. Which search is most directly aimed at this specific risk?
options: A drainage and water search
An environmental search
A chancel repair search
The LLC1 search alone
interaction.trapExplanation: Drainage searches address mains connections and sewer routes, not historical contamination — a former dry cleaner's is a textbook contaminated land risk (solvents used in the cleaning process), which is squarely what an environmental search screens for.
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right — former dry cleaning use is a recognised contamination risk, which environmental searches are specifically designed to screen for.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Think about what a dry cleaner's actually uses (chemical solvents) rather than what utilities it needs — that points to contamination risk, not drainage.

testPool.prompt: A solicitor wants to confirm whether a financial charge has been registered by the local authority against a property. Which search reveals this?
options: LLC1
CON29DW
An environmental search
A chancel repair search
testPool.explanation: Registered financial charges are a classic local land charge, revealed by an LLC1 search of the Local Land Charges Register.

testPool.prompt: Which standard form is used to raise the local authority's general enquiries about roads, planning enforcement and conservation area status?
options: CON29
LLC1
TA6
CON29O
testPool.explanation: CON29 (Enquiries of Local Authority) is the standard set of general questions; CON29O is the optional additional set used where a specific risk warrants it, and LLC1 searches the formal register rather than asking questions.

testPool.prompt: What best distinguishes an LLC1 search result from a CON29 answer?
options: LLC1 answers are always more expensive to obtain

An LLC1 entry reflects a formally registered charge and a missed entry carries a statutory compensation right; a CON29 answer is the authority's best information and does not carry the same statutory guarantee
CON29 is only used for commercial property transactions
LLC1 searches cover planning permissions, while CON29 covers only tree preservation orders
testPool.trapExplanation: Students sometimes assume the two forms carry identical legal weight because they are submitted together on one form. They protect different things: LLC1 sits behind a statutory register with a compensation right for a missed entry; CON29 answers do not.
testPool.explanation: Keeping the statutory register (LLC1) distinct from the local authority's general enquiry answers (CON29) is central to advising a client accurately on what a clean search actually guarantees.

testPool.prompt: A client wants to build a single-storey rear extension and is worried about whether a public sewer runs under the proposed footprint. Which search should the solicitor prioritise for this specific concern?
options: A chancel repair search
A drainage and water search
An LLC1 search alone
A Misrepresentation Act enquiry to the seller
testPool.explanation: The route of public sewers relative to a property, and whether building over or near one requires water company consent, is precisely what a drainage and water search is designed to reveal.

testPool.prompt: A buyer is purchasing a property built on the site of a former petrol filling station, now redeveloped as housing thirty years ago. What is the most directly relevant search?
options: A drainage and water search
A chancel repair search
An environmental search assessing contaminated land risk from the historical use
No search is needed since the site has been redeveloped
testPool.explanation: Former petrol station use is a classic prompt for an environmental search, since underground fuel storage can leave residual contamination long after redevelopment.

testPool.prompt: What does a chancel repair search actually investigate?
options: Whether the property has ever suffered structural roof damage
Whether the land has a historical connection to rectorial glebe land that could carry liability to contribute to the parish church's chancel repair
Whether the property is within a conservation area affecting church buildings
Whether planning permission was granted for any nearby church extension
testPool.trapExplanation: The word 'chancel' misleads some students into thinking this is about the physical condition of the property's own roof. It is an entirely separate, historical liability tied to old rectorial land ownership, unconnected to the property's actual structure.
testPool.explanation: Chancel repair liability is a genuinely obscure historical liability that can attach to land with no visible connection to a church at all, which is exactly why a targeted search (or indemnity insurance) is used rather than relying on a viewing.

testPool.prompt: A search reveals a potential chancel repair liability affecting a property in an older parish. What is the conventional practical response for a buyer's solicitor?
options: Refuse to proceed with the purchase under any circumstances
Advise the client to obtain chancel repair indemnity insurance rather than pursuing further historical investigation
Report the matter to the local authority for removal from the register
Treat it as irrelevant since chancel repair liability was abolished nationally
testPool.explanation: Where a chancel repair risk is identified, indemnity insurance is the standard, cost-effective practical solution, rather than exhaustive historical investigation of parish records.

testPool.prompt: On which standard form does a seller typically answer pre-contract enquiries about matters such as disputes, boundaries and past building works?
options: TA6 (Property Information Form)
LLC1
CON29DW
The title plan
testPool.explanation: The TA6 Property Information Form is the standard vehicle for the seller's own pre-contract answers, covering matters no public search could reveal.

testPool.prompt: A seller answers 'No' on the TA6 form to a question about disputes with neighbours, honestly forgetting a boundary dispute that was resolved informally two years earlier. The buyer only discovers this after completion, when the dispute resurfaces and causes them loss. What is the correct legal characterisation?
options: No claim is possible because the seller did not act dishonestly

This may still amount to an actionable misrepresentation under the Misrepresentation Act 1967, since honesty is not required for liability, though the available remedies differ from a fraudulent misrepresentation
The buyer's only remedy is to sue the seller's solicitor for negligence
The answer cannot be a misrepresentation because it was given on a standard form rather than in a private conversation
testPool.trapExplanation: Many students assume dishonesty is required for any misrepresentation claim to succeed. It is not — an innocent misrepresentation can still ground a claim, though remedies (particularly damages) are more limited than for a fraudulent or negligent misrepresentation.
testPool.explanation: The seller's state of mind (fraudulent, negligent or innocent) affects the remedies available, not whether a misrepresentation occurred at all — a false statement of fact that induced the contract is enough to engage the Act.

testPool.prompt: An LLC1 search fails to reveal a registered planning enforcement notice due to an error by the registering authority, and the buyer suffers loss as a result after purchase. What does s 10 of the Local Land Charges Act 1975 provide?
options: No compensation is available because LLC1 searches are advisory only
A statutory right to compensation for the loss suffered as a consequence of the failure to reveal the subsisting registered charge
The buyer must instead pursue a claim in misrepresentation against the seller
The enforcement notice ceases to have effect once missed from a search
testPool.explanation: Section 10 creates a specific statutory compensation right where an official search fails to reveal a charge that was in fact registered, distinguishing LLC1 from the non-statutory character of CON29 answers.

testPool.prompt: Which piece of legislation governs the register searched by an LLC1 form?
options: The Land Registration Act 2002
The Local Land Charges Act 1975
The Misrepresentation Act 1967
The Law of Property Act 1925
testPool.explanation: The Local Land Charges Act 1975 establishes and governs the register that LLC1 searches — a different statutory regime from the Land Registration Act 2002, which governs the register of title itself.

testPool.prompt: A CON29 answer states there are no known road proposals affecting a property, but the answer is simply wrong because the local authority's own file was incomplete, with no registered charge involved. Compared to a missed LLC1 entry, how does the buyer's position differ?
options: Identical — both carry the same statutory compensation right
Weaker — CON29 answers are not backed by the same statutory compensation regime as a registered local land charge missed from LLC1
Stronger — CON29 answers carry additional statutory protection LLC1 does not
There is no meaningful difference in practice between the two
testPool.explanation: This is the core distinction this lesson tests: an LLC1 miss engages the s 10 compensation right because it concerns a genuinely registered charge; a wrong CON29 answer, however unhelpful, does not carry that same statutory backing.

testPool.prompt: Why is it inaccurate to describe the standard local authority search bundle as simply 'clean' or 'not clean' in advice to a client?
options: Because it is never possible to describe search results in summary form
Because LLC1 and CON29 answer genuinely different questions with different legal weight, and collapsing them into one label obscures what the client is actually protected against
Because local authority searches are always inaccurate and therefore unreliable to summarise
Because the terms 'clean' and 'not clean' are prohibited by the Law Society
testPool.trapExplanation: The trap is assuming this is a stylistic quibble rather than a substantive one — the point is that a single summary label hides the real difference between a statutorily-guaranteed register entry and a non-statutory local authority answer, which matters if either turns out to be wrong.
testPool.explanation: Accurate advice distinguishes the statutory guarantee behind LLC1 from the non-statutory nature of CON29 answers, so the client understands exactly what recourse (if any) exists if something is later found to be wrong.

testPool.prompt: A property borders a river with a documented history of flooding nearby. The buyer's solicitor orders only a standard local authority search and skips any further enquiry. Is this an adequate response to the described risk?
options: Yes, the local authority search always covers flood risk in full
No, a flood-prone location calls for an environmental search with flood-risk screening in addition to the standard local authority search
No, only a chancel repair search addresses flood risk near a river
Yes, provided the seller confirms in conversation that the property has never flooded
testPool.explanation: Flood risk is specifically the domain of an environmental search's flood-screening element, not the standard local authority search — relying on the local search alone, or on the seller's informal assurance, falls short of the risk actually described.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The recurring trap in this lesson is treating pre-contract searches and enquiries as an undifferentiated checklist. Each search answers a distinct, narrow question, LLC1 and CON29 carry different legal weight, and a seller's inaccurate answer on the TA6 form is a live misrepresentation risk, not a harmless formality.
